source.title: MINAR: Mechanistic Interpretability for Neural Algorithmic Reasoning
source.authors: Jesse He; Helen Jenne; Max Vargas; Davis Brown; Gal Mishne; Yu-Su Wang; Henry Kvinge

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It directly examines delayed generalization and circuit changes over training in algorithmic GNNs, but uses a different model, task, and measures from the original grokking setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that the full Bellman-Ford model generalizes almost immediately, then analyzes how its circuit changes during continued L1-regularized training. Those results bear on V1, V2, and aspects of V5. It also compares circuits across initializations for V6. The CLRS circuit-fidelity and overlap results and the BFS shortcut result do not bear on the listed versions. Cited results from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper's main aim is circuit discovery in GNNs. Its Bellman-Ford case study reports, as a result in a new algorithmic setting (shortest paths on graphs), that the full model shows no generalization delay. It also tracks circuit sparsification after generalization and compares circuits across seeds. These results bear on V1, V2 and V6. The task, model and loss-based measures differ from the originals, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also present MINAR as recovering faithful circuits, and link delayed pruning to grokking and model compression. They say the final circuit's parameters 'generalize later than the full model'. They contrast this with vestigial-circuit accounts: the early extra parameters are necessary, not memorizing.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a two-layer minimum-aggregated GNN trained on shortest-path graph tasks with L1 regularization, rather than the original modular-arithmetic setup. It evaluates losses and extracted circuits, not a delayed train/test accuracy jump or a training-set-size sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Self-loops change the timing of circuit generalization: the paper reports around epoch 3000 for the mainline circuit and around epoch 18000 without self-loops. Initializations change which neurons appear in the circuit, while the authors report functional identity across runs.

fits_no_version.finding: After generalization, L1 regularization refines an already-generalizing circuit into a sparser one; this happens without any memorizing or vestigial circuit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization-driven delayed circuit sparsification can occur after prompt generalization, without a memorization phase or grokking-like behavioral delay.

record.problems: The Bellman-Ford delayed-circuit analysis is primarily reported for a single run; additional initializations are shown, but no uncertainty estimates are given. There is no unregularized comparison or training-set-size sweep. Bellman-Ford results use test losses rather than training/test accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results omitted under the row limit. SALSA-CLRS circuit-fidelity/overlap results and the parallel BFS shortcut analysis are outside the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Accuracy jump from chance, dependence of the delay on training-set size, and the modular-arithmetic setting.
The Fourier algorithm, progress measures anticipating a behavioral jump, and removal of memorizing components (none were observed).
All parts: non-algorithmic data, initialization-scale or weight-norm switching.
All parts: no memorization competitor, no regularization control, no critical dataset size, no ungrokking.
Variation across architectures and hyperparameters; only seeds of one designed setup were compared.
All parts: no optimizer or floating-point controls.

missing.what: Delayed circuit generalization replicated across four additional seeds; the paper says the same behavior is observed.
Parallel Bellman-Ford+BFS circuits are functionally the same across four seeds.

record.verdict_notes: Training uses AdamW with weight decay 0.01 plus L1 regularization (η=0.001), not L1 alone. Measures are losses, not accuracies. The grokking-relevant analysis is mainly a single run, with seed plots but no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report training accuracy, chance-level test accuracy, a test-accuracy jump, or a sweep over training-set sizes.

It does not track the specific Fourier algorithm or show continuous progress measures anticipating a behavioral jump. It does not show memorizing components being removed; the authors describe the extra early circuit parameters as necessary.
No non-algorithmic data or initialization-scale/weight-norm sweep testing a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
No controlled comparison of regularization regimes, critical dataset size, or ungrokking below a dataset-size threshold.
The comparison is across initializations of the Bellman-Ford GNN, not across architectures or hyperparameters.
No test of adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifacts.

rows.subject: Bellman-Ford MinAggGNN
rows.operation_detail: Train with L1 sparsity regularization and track full-model train and test losses over epochs.

conditions.value: curated small graphs of size up to 6 nodes
300 randomly generated graphs; up to 200 nodes

rows.measure: Full-model generalization timing; final reported train and test losses
rows.value: The authors state that the full model generalizes almost immediately, almost simultaneously with training-loss convergence, and performs well on the test set after only about 1000 epochs; train loss LMSE = 0.0001 and test loss LMult = 0.0578.
rows.note: The reported measure is loss, not accuracy. The authors explicitly contrast this prompt full-model generalization with later generalization of the extracted circuit.
rows.check: Generalization happening almost simultaneously with training-loss convergence means no delay; it is not the opposite effect, so the state is absent, not reversed. R1 measures full-model timing only, so it does not bear on V2. Conditions omit AdamW weight decay 0.01, which is used alongside L1 (Appendix D).

rows.subject: Bellman-Ford MinAggGNN circuit at epoch 1000
rows.operation_detail: Extract and evaluate a circuit from an intermediate training checkpoint.
rows.note: The paper describes this as a sufficient, generalizable circuit; it is larger than the final circuit.
rows.check: A sufficient generalizing circuit (73 edges) already exists at epoch 1000, when the full model generalizes. The link to V5 is dropped: there is no memorization competitor and no regularization control.

source_check.correct: State: partial for V2. The epoch-1000 circuit is sufficient and generalizable, with 73 edges and LMult = 0.0578; this does not establish the full gradual-formation and memorization-removal mechanism.
source_check.problem: Observed overstates the evidence for V2; an early sufficient circuit establishes only part of that mechanism.

rows.subject: Bellman-Ford MinAggGNN trained without self-loops
rows.operation_detail: Track full-model and extracted-circuit generalization during L1-regularized training without self-loops.
rows.measure: Full-model and circuit test generalization timing
rows.baseline: Full model achieves strong generalization early
rows.value: The final circuit does not generalize until around epoch 18000; the full model achieves strong generalization early. Final reported full-model losses are train LMSE = 0.0002 and test LMult = 0.0642; the circuit test LMult is 0.0599.
rows.note: The paper says an epoch-10000 circuit has 20 edges; the late generalization timing is described in text, while the curves are plotted.
rows.check: For V1 the full model generalizes early, so the delay is absent rather than reversed. For V2 the result is partial: the late pruning near epoch 18000 (20 edges at epoch 10000, 17 in the final circuit) removes parts of the minimum operation, not memorizing parts. This row mixes two measures and should be split.

source_check.correct: States: absent for V1; partial for V2. The full model generalizes early. The final circuit generalizes around epoch 18000; connections pruned from the earlier circuit participate in the minimum operation.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix A.3, discussion preceding Figure 13 and Figures 12–14.
source_check.problem: A single absent state does not fit both linked versions; V2 has partial mechanistic evidence.

rows.subject: Bellman-Ford MinAggGNN across four additional initializations
rows.operation_detail: Compare the identified circuits across different initializations.
rows.measure: Functional identity of identified circuits across runs
rows.value: Each additional circuit is described as functionally identical to the mainline circuit, but uses different neurons.
rows.note: This supports sameness of the identified function across initializations only; the paper does not test architecture or hyperparameter variation.
rows.check: Functional identity is a qualitative statement. LMult values are given only for seeds 1 and 2 in the extracted text. The training setup is designed to force Bellman-Ford (Nerem et al.), so convergence to it is expected.

relation.reason: Its own training trajectories, checkpoint circuits and repeated initializations bear on the claim versions.

tranche.reason: The study reports generalization timing and circuit-pruning results in a new algorithmic setting: shortest-path MinAggGNNs.

source_check.notes: Appendix D specifies AdamW, weight decay 0.01 and L1 coefficient 0.001. The full-model baseline LMult = 0.0578 is the reported trained-model result, not an explicitly matched baseline for each intermediate checkpoint.

statements.correction: Section 5.2: circuit LMult = 0.0545; removing the circuit yields LMult = 21870.6836. Appendix A.1 compares circuit-discovery scoring methods. Appendix A.4.1 reports functionally identical circuits across four additional initializations; architecture and hyperparameter variation are untested.
statements.problem: The circuit-repeatability claim is accurate, but the unqualified assertion that the GNN study has no controls overlooks circuit-removal ablations and scoring-method baselines.
